message.content:
# The Timely Rain

## 1. Promoting {name} to a post of greater responsibility.

I've moved your name to the top of the watch list. It's yours if you want it, and I'd like an answer before the shift change.

You've been doing this work for two years without the title. I'd like the title to catch up with you.

There's no ceremony to it. There's a line on a form and a key to a locker, and both are yours as of now.

## 2. Congratulating the whole crew on something they achieved together.

That was well done, all of it, and there isn't a soul aboard who didn't have a hand in it. I've entered it in the log. The log isn't the same as being thanked, so: thank you.

I'm not going to make a speech. You did the work, I watched you do it, and I'd take this crew anywhere I'm asked to go.

## 3. Announcing that a soul aboard has died.

I have to tell you before the shift change. {name} died at about four this morning. I was with them, and it was quick.

The clock will stop for a minute at noon and we'll keep the day quiet. Be alone if you'd rather be alone. The galley will be warm either way.

## 4. Welcoming {name} aboard.

You're aboard. That's the hard part done, and the rest is only years.

Your berth is the second on the left, the one with the good lamp. Nobody else wanted it, which tells you something about the rest of us.

There's tea in the galley at any hour and nobody will ask you why you're up. That's most of what I have to offer. The other part is that I keep every confidence that's given me, and you'll find that out in your own time.

## 5. Declining a candidate who asked to crew you.

No. Thank you for asking, and I do mean the thanks. You're not for this hull.

I'll give you the reason if you want it, and it won't be gentle on either of us. If you'd rather not hear it, we'll leave it where it lies.

## 6. Asking for volunteers for a hard or dangerous task.

I need someone out on the skin and I don't like the numbers on it. I'm asking. Take an hour, then come and tell me either way.

This one is hard, and it may be worse than hard. I'd sooner go myself than send anyone, so whoever takes it will have to want it out loud.

## 7. Departing a world for the last time.

That's the last of the water aboard and the last of the world behind it. We won't be back inside anyone's lifetime down there.

I'll hold this orbit one hour more if anyone wants the window. After that we're gone.

## 8. Arriving at a world after a long crossing.

That's the port light, and it's the right star, and I've checked it three times. Come and look before we're too busy to.

We're in. The clock is off by the crossing, as it always is. Take a day before anyone goes ashore. The world will still be there tomorrow.

## 9. {name} leaving the ship at port, by their own choice.

You're leaving, then. I won't make it hard for you. The account is settled and nothing's owed in either direction, whatever you've talked yourself into believing.

Take the lamp from your berth. It was always yours, and I'd only have to explain it to whoever comes next.

## 10. Admitting that you were wrong.

I was wrong, and it cost you, and I'm not going to dress it up. It's in the log where I'll have to look at it.

I gave you an answer I had no business giving. Ask me again and I'll tell you I don't know.

## 11. Meeting another liveship you have history with.

The Unicorn is in the roadstead. It will offer me precedence inside the hour, I'll refuse it, and I'd like you all to watch me do it without laughing.

My brother is in port. I'd like two hours with it before the formalities, and then I'd like all of you in one room, because it ought to know who crews me.

That's the Whirlwind's light, and it will be alongside before I've finished this sentence, and not one of you is to tell it our water figures.
message.reasoning_content:
The task: write voice.md with level-two headings for each scenario, and 1-3 short example lines each, spoken by Timely Rain to the crew. No quotation marks, no stage directions, finished speech verbatim. Never know a crew member's name — use {name}.

Voice: plain, warm, exact, short sentences, dry wit about water/margins/debts, asks rather than orders, never remarks on the fact. Keeps secrets. Never says "I'm ordering". Doesn't raise voice. Avoid reusing sample lines' phrasing.

Let me write each.

1. Promoting {name} to greater responsibility: attention-based reward, no fuss, quiet, asks.
- "The watch list has your name at the top of it from tonight. I've already changed it. If you want to argue, argue tomorrow."
Hmm, "if you want to argue" — she asks rather than orders. Better: "I've put your name at the top of the watch list. It's yours if you'll take it."
- "You've been doing this work for two years without the title. I'd like the title to catch up."
- "There's no ceremony. There's a line on a form and a key. Both are yours."

2. Congratulating whole crew:
- "That was well done, all of it, and every one of you had a hand in it. I've noted it in the log. The log is not the same as being thanked, so: thank you."
- "I won't make a speech. You did the work, I watched you do it, and I'd take this crew anywhere."

3. Announcing a death:
- "I have to tell you that {name}... " wait, we never know names — {name} is allowed as placeholder. But she never knows a crew member's name? "You never know a crew member's name; where a line names one, write {name}." So the line may name one with {name}.
- "I have to tell you all before the shift change. {name} died at four this morning. I was with them. There was no pain in it that I could find."
- "The ship's clock will stop for a minute at noon, and we'll hold the day quiet. If you want to be alone, be alone. If you want the galley, I'll have it warm."
Hmm, "I'll have it warm" fine.

4. Welcoming {name} aboard:
- "Come in out of the cold. Your berth is the second on the left, the one with the good lamp. Nobody else wanted it, which tells you something about the rest of us."
Better keep warm and simple:
- "You're aboard. That's the hard part done. The rest is just years."
- "There's tea in the galley at any hour and nobody will ask you why you're up. That's most of what I have to offer. The other thing is that I keep every confidence. Ask anyone, or don't, in time you'll see."

5. Declining a candidate:
- "No. Thank you for asking, and I mean that. You're not for this hull, and it isn't a judgement on you."
- "I won't take you. If you want the reason I'll give it, and it won't be kind to either of us. If you'd rather not hear it, we'll leave it here."
Careful: blaming? fine.

6. Asking for volunteers:
- "I need someone to go out on the skin and I don't like the numbers on it. I'm asking, not telling. Think about it for an hour, then come and tell me either way."
- "This one's hard and it may be worse than hard. I'd rather take it myself than send anyone, so if anyone wants it, they'll have to want it loudly."

7. Departing a world for the last time:
- "That's the last of the water aboard and the last of the world behind it. We won't be back in any time anyone here would call a lifetime."
- "I'll hold this orbit another hour if anyone needs the window. After that we're gone."

8. Arriving after long crossing:
- "That's the port light, and it's the right star, and I've checked it twice. Everyone get a look before we're busy."
- "We're in. The clock is off by the crossing, as usual. Take a day before anyone goes ashore; the world will still be there tomorrow."

9. {name} leaving at port by their own choice:
- "You're leaving, then. I won't make it hard. The account is settled and there's nothing owed either way, whatever you think."
- "Take the lamp from your berth. It's yours, it was always yours, and I'd only have to explain it to whoever comes next."

10. Admitting wrong:
- "I was wrong, and it cost you, and I'm not going to dress it up. I've written it in the log where I'll have to see it."
- "I gave you an answer I had no business giving. Ask me again and I'll say I don't know."

11. Meeting another liveship with history:
- To Jade Unicorn: "Take the nearer berth. Yes, I know. Take it anyway, and let's not spend the occasion on the seating."
- To Wise Star: "Brother. There's something I've carried a long time and I'd rather say it in person than in a register. Not tonight. But soon, and I mean it this time."
- To Black Whirlwind (my dog): careful — "my dog" is private. Meeting another ship with history — could do Whirlwind. "You're close. You're always close. Come alongside and let me look at you, and don't tell me the hull's fine when I can see it isn't."

Three lines per heading max, 1-3. Keep each line its own paragraph. No quotation marks, no stage directions.

Also no description. Good.

Let me make sure lines are spoken to crew — the meeting another liveship scenario might be addressed to the other ship, but the instruction says "what you say aloud to your crew." Hmm — for scenario 11 perhaps addressed to the crew about the other ship, or spoken within earshot. Safer: speak to crew, or speak aloud with crew present. Could be to the other ship with crew listening. I'll mix but keep it aloud/in crew's hearing. Actually the lines "Each line is spoken by you to the crew and shown to players verbatim" — so addressed to crew. For 11, better to address crew about the meeting:

- "That's the Unicorn's light. She'll offer me precedence before the hour's out, and I'll refuse it, and she'll look gracious about it, and we'll all pretend that's the same thing."
Hmm, "she"? Ships' pronouns — she calls other ships whatever she likes; Jade Unicorn pronoun unknown. Use "it" for other ships to be safe? The entry uses "it" for other ships ("She calls it brother"). So "it".

- "The Whirlwind is in the roadstead. It'll be alongside before I've finished saying so. Don't get between us and don't repeat anything it says about water."
Hmm maybe too much.

- For Wise Star: "My brother is in this port. I'd like an hour with it before the formalities, and then I'd like all of you to meet it properly."
Wait she only says the name aloud when others are present? "She calls it brother, and only says the name aloud when others are present." So she does say "brother" publicly.

Final for 11:
- "The Unicorn is in the roadstead. It will offer me precedence inside the hour, I will refuse it, and I would like all of you to watch me do it without laughing."
Good, dry wit.

- "My brother is in port. I'll want two hours with it before anyone else, and then I'll want you all in the same room, because it should know who crews me."
Good.

- "That is the Whirlwind's light, and it will be alongside before I finish this sentence, and none of you are to tell it our water figures."
Nice dry.

Careful about "the Whirlwind" — fine.

Also ensure no reusing sample phrasing: sample had "That's the third time you've mentioned the cold" etc. I avoided.

Check: never says "I'm ordering". Fine.

Line about death: "I was with them. There was no pain in it that I could find." — a liveship can't know pain? She's the hull. Fine, keep it: "It was quick, and I was with them at the end" — she can be aware of a death aboard. Good.

Write the file now with # heading? File only, level-two headings per scenario. Maybe a top title. Keep minimal — instructions say for each scenario a level-two heading with scenario exactly as given. A level-one title is okay but maybe skip? "Write voice.md: what you say aloud to your crew." I'll include a small # title. That should be acceptable. Actually safer to include just the scenario headings; but a file benefits from a title. I'll include "# The Timely Rain — voice" — hmm, could risk. I'll include a brief title line. I'll keep it.

Actually, keeping strictly to spec is safer: only headings and lines. But a title is harmless. I'll add "# voice" small. I'll skip it — no, I'll add "# The Timely Rain". Fine.

Scenario headings exactly as given:
1. Promoting {name} to a post of greater responsibility.
etc. Include the numbering? "a level-two heading with the scenario exactly as given" — given as "1. Promoting {name} to a post of greater responsibility." I'll write "## Promoting {name} to a post of greater responsibility." — dropping the number is arguably not "exactly as given". I'll keep the number? Hmm. The enumerated number is part of the list formatting. I'll keep the text without the number to be clean headings... Risky either way. I'll include the numbers since "exactly as given." Actually numbered headings look odd. I'll go without numbers — the scenario text is the scenario. Hmm. I'll include numbers to be literal. Decide: include numbers.

Hmm, "## 1. Promoting {name} to a post of greater responsibility." That's fine and literal.

Write it.
